summary:
Russia offers no route to legal gender recognition. A law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents. A trans visitor's passport, visa and identity papers therefore remain as issued, and no Russian procedure exists to align them with the holder's gender.

The Supreme Court designated the non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist in November 2023. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions by June 2025 for alleged participation in the movement or display of its symbols, with charges brought under both administrative and criminal codes. Arrests have followed for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Between March and May 2026 nine organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The propaganda statutes reach expression. The 2013 law covered material concerning minors; a December 2022 amendment extended it to all age groups, and it now prohibits material promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships and material that gives minors a "desire to change their sex". More than 180 enforcement cases were opened in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined, with fines of about 26 million rubles. Meduza reported in June 2025 that propaganda cases had grown eighteenfold over the previous decade and that fines under the statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in two years.

Enforcement has reached venues. Within 48 hours of the November 2023 designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face the walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported in June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through the year.

Detention carries lethal risk. In December 2024 a Russian man arrested on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Russian law provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and motivation by sexual orientation or gender identity is not an aggravating factor in sentencing. The government does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Partner recognition is unavailable. Neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions exist, and a 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage. The European Court of Human Rights held in Fedotova and Others v. Russia (2021) that the absence of any legal recognition for same-sex relationships violated the convention; Russia left the court in 2022. The 2023 gender-transition law deems a marriage void where a trans person marries someone of their same birth sex, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognised status.

The US State Department maintains a Level 4, Do Not Travel advisory for Russia that includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers.

Public attitudes are hostile. A 2022 survey found 74% of Russians said homosexuality should not be accepted by society, up from 60% in 2002, and a September 2021 survey showed support for equal rights for gays and lesbians had fallen to 33%.
tangentialFactors:
A UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, issued in June 2025 and updated in August 2026, treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Emigration has become a route out. Foreign Policy reported in August 2024 that the extremism designation drove a purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians, and Novaya Gazeta Europe reported in June 2024 that emigration had become the only means of survival for many transgender Russians, profiling those caught in limbo between leaving and staying.

AP reported in December 2024 that Russia's LGBTQ+ community was living in fear after the new laws and court rulings, pushed into silence, flight and self-censorship. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing.
localsOnly:
The 2023 law deprives people diagnosed with gender dysphoria of the right to adopt children. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions.

BBC Russian reported in July 2024 on a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk. She was held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and do manual labour, and escaped when police responded to a phone she found.

Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, and in 2010 Russia was fined by the European Court of Human Rights for systematically refusing pride parade permits.

A queer woman in St Petersburg described waking up to find herself "a second-class citizen" after the Supreme Court's extremist designation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how Russian border guards or police handle a traveller whose appearance does not match the gender marker on their documents, or whether secondary screening of trans travellers occurs at entry.

Whether the 2023 prohibition on changing gender markers applies to documents issued by foreign states, and how Russian authorities treat a visitor holding a foreign passport with a changed marker, is not addressed by the sources reviewed.

No inventory source gives a count of prosecutions or convictions of foreign nationals under the extremism or propaganda statutes.
